nutrients.label: Energy
nutrients.why: How much energy the food releases when the body burns it. Per 100 g it says as much about water content as about the food, since cooked grains and pulses are mostly water.

nutrients.label: Protein
nutrients.why: Supplies the amino acids the body rebuilds into its own tissue, enzymes and antibodies. Quantity is only half of it: the amino acid columns show whether the mix is usable.

nutrients.label: Carbohydrate
nutrients.why: The body's most readily used fuel, arriving in whole plant foods with the fibre and minerals still attached. Measured by difference, so this figure includes both the fibre and the sugars below it.

nutrients.label: Fibre
nutrients.why: The part of a plant human enzymes cannot break down, which is why it reaches the gut bacteria intact. It slows glucose absorption and feeds the microbiome, and most diets fall short of it.

nutrients.label: Sugars
nutrients.why: The sugars inside the carbohydrate total, whether naturally present or added. In whole fruit they come bound up with fibre and water, which is why they behave differently from the same amount in a drink.

nutrients.label: Total fat
nutrients.why: The most energy-dense nutrient, and the vehicle for vitamins A, D, E and K, none of which the body absorbs well from a fat-free meal. Which kind of fat matters more than how much.

nutrients.label: Saturated fat
nutrients.why: The fraction with no double bonds, solid at room temperature. Plant foods are generally low in it, coconut and palm being the exceptions, and it is the fraction dietary guidance asks people to limit.

nutrients.label: Water
nutrients.why: How much of 100 g is simply water. It is the main reason cooked and dry forms of one food look so different: a cooked grain is mostly water, so everything else in the row is diluted.

nutrients.label: Omega-3 (ALA)
nutrients.why: The only omega-3 the body cannot make, and the form plant foods supply. Conversion into the long-chain EPA and DHA that the brain and eyes actually use is inefficient, so a high ALA intake is not the same thing.

nutrients.label: Omega-3 (EPA)
nutrients.why: Eicosapentaenoic acid, 20:5, the long-chain omega-3 that ALA is meant to convert into and one of the two the body actually uses. Conversion from ALA is poor, and it is close to absent from plant foods: of the foods here that USDA assayed, four carry any at all.

nutrients.label: Omega-3 (DHA)
nutrients.why: Docosahexaenoic acid, 22:6, the omega-3 that makes up much of the brain and the retina. Plant foods essentially do not contain it: USDA assayed most of the foods here and found it above zero in one. Algal oil is the vegan source, since algae is where fish get it too.

nutrients.label: Omega-6 (LA)
nutrients.why: The essential omega-6, plentiful in nuts, seeds and their oils. It competes with ALA for the same conversion enzymes, so a very high intake makes the little omega-3 conversion there is smaller still.

nutrients.label: Omega-7 (palmitoleic)
nutrients.why: A monounsaturated fat concentrated in macadamias and sea buckthorn. Not essential, since the body makes its own, and counted inside the monounsaturated total rather than in addition to it.

nutrients.label: Omega-9 (oleic)
nutrients.why: The main monounsaturated fat, and what makes olive oil what it is. The body can make it, so it is not essential, but replacing saturated fat with it is one of the better-supported dietary swaps.

nutrients.label: Monounsaturated
nutrients.why: Fats with a single double bond, the omega-9 and omega-7 columns included. Stable enough to cook with, and the fraction Mediterranean diets are richest in.

nutrients.label: Polyunsaturated
nutrients.why: Fats with more than one double bond, including both of the essential fatty acids. They oxidise readily with heat and light, which is why cold-pressed seed oils need more careful handling.

nutrients.label: Lauric (12:0)
nutrients.why: The 12-carbon saturated fat that coconut is largely made of and that is close to absent everywhere else. It raises LDL cholesterol but raises HDL alongside it, which is why coconut sits awkwardly in the usual saturated fat story.

nutrients.label: Palmitic (16:0)
nutrients.why: The most abundant saturated fat in both plants and animals, and the one dietary advice about saturated fat is mostly about. It is the fraction most consistently shown to raise LDL cholesterol.

nutrients.label: Stearic (18:0)
nutrients.why: The 18-carbon saturated fat of cocoa butter and shea. The body converts much of it into oleic acid, so unlike the shorter saturated fats it leaves LDL cholesterol roughly where it found it.

nutrients.label: Histidine
nutrients.why: Essential, and the starting point for histamine, which the immune system and the stomach both run on. It also buffers the acid that builds up in working muscle.

nutrients.label: Isoleucine
nutrients.why: One of the three branched-chain amino acids, burned in the muscle itself rather than sent to the liver first. It also has a hand in haemoglobin production and glucose uptake.

nutrients.label: Leucine
nutrients.why: The branched-chain amino acid that signals muscle to start building protein, which is why it is the one strength athletes count. Soy, pulses and seeds are the richest plant sources.

nutrients.label: Lysine
nutrients.why: Essential, needed for collagen and for carrying fat into the mitochondria to be burned. It is the one cereals run short on, and precisely what pulses supply.

nutrients.label: Methionine
nutrients.why: Essential, and the starting point for every methylation reaction in the body. Pulses are usually short of it, which is what grains, nuts and seeds make up for.

nutrients.label: Cysteine
nutrients.why: Not essential in itself, because the body makes it from methionine, but every gram eaten is a gram of methionine saved. It carries the sulphur in glutathione, the body's own main antioxidant.

nutrients.label: Phenylalanine
nutrients.why: Essential, and the raw material for tyrosine and everything downstream of it. Scored as a pair with tyrosine because the conversion only runs one way.

nutrients.label: Tyrosine
nutrients.why: Made from phenylalanine, and the precursor of dopamine, adrenaline and thyroid hormone. Not essential so long as phenylalanine is plentiful, which is why the two are scored together.

nutrients.label: Threonine
nutrients.why: Essential, and used heavily in the mucus lining the gut and in the collagen and elastin holding tissue together. Losses through the gut are large, so more is needed than body tissue alone suggests.

nutrients.label: Tryptophan
nutrients.why: Essential, and the precursor of serotonin, melatonin and some of the body's own niacin. It is the scarcest essential amino acid in nearly every food, which is why the requirement for it is the lowest.

nutrients.label: Valine
nutrients.why: The third branched-chain amino acid, used in muscle for energy and repair. Like the other two it is burned where it lands rather than processed by the liver first.

nutrients.label: Arginine
nutrients.why: Not essential for a healthy adult, but the sole source of nitric oxide, which is what relaxes blood vessels. Nuts, seeds and pulses are the richest plant sources.

nutrients.label: Alanine
nutrients.why: Not essential. Muscle uses it to ship spare nitrogen to the liver, which turns the carbon back into glucose, a loop that keeps blood sugar up through long exercise.

nutrients.label: Aspartic acid
nutrients.why: Not essential. It feeds the urea cycle that disposes of surplus nitrogen, and is a building block of the purines in DNA.

nutrients.label: Glutamic acid
nutrients.why: The most abundant amino acid in most proteins, and the brain's main excitatory signal. It is also what gives tomatoes, mushrooms and soy sauce their savoury taste.

nutrients.label: Glycine
nutrients.why: The smallest amino acid, a third of all the collagen in the body, and one of the three the body needs to make creatine. Plant diets tend to supply less of it than omnivorous ones.

nutrients.label: Proline
nutrients.why: Not essential. It is what makes collagen kink the way it does, so skin, connective tissue and blood vessel walls all depend on it.

nutrients.label: Serine
nutrients.why: Not essential. It goes into cell membranes and into the one-carbon pathway that folate and B12 also feed, which ties it to methylation.

nutrients.label: Vitamin A
nutrients.why: Runs vision in dim light, keeps skin and mucous membranes intact and directs part of the immune response. Plant foods contain no retinol, only carotenoids the body converts, and this figure already counts that conversion.

nutrients.label: Vitamin C
nutrients.why: Needed to build collagen, which is why scurvy is a disease of missing fruit and veg. It also multiplies the absorption of plant iron eaten in the same meal, which matters more on a plant-based diet.

nutrients.label: Vitamin D2
nutrients.why: Governs how much calcium the gut takes up, so bone depends on it as much as on calcium itself. Almost no plant food contains any: skin makes it from sunlight, and at high latitudes that stops in winter.

nutrients.label: Vitamin E
nutrients.why: The main antioxidant inside cell membranes, where it protects the polyunsaturated fats from oxidising. Nuts, seeds and their oils are the plant sources that count.

nutrients.label: Gamma-tocopherol
nutrients.why: The vitamin E form that dominates in seeds and most nuts, often several times the alpha figure beside it. It carries no daily value and the body excretes it faster, so it is not counted as vitamin E, but it is not nothing either.

nutrients.label: Vitamin K
nutrients.why: Activates the proteins that bind calcium into bone and that clot blood. Dark leafy greens supply it in quantity, and it needs some fat in the meal to be absorbed.

nutrients.label: Thiamin (B1)
nutrients.why: Releases energy from carbohydrate, so the more carbohydrate a diet carries the more of it gets used. Nerve tissue is what fails first without it.

nutrients.label: Riboflavin (B2)
nutrients.why: Part of the two coenzymes that carry electrons through energy metabolism, so almost nothing burns fuel without it. It is one of the nutrients plant-based diets can quietly run low on.

nutrients.label: Niacin (B3)
nutrients.why: Underpins the coenzymes behind several hundred reactions, from releasing energy to repairing DNA. The body also makes some from tryptophan, so a good protein intake covers part of the need.

nutrients.label: Pantothenic acid (B5)
nutrients.why: The core of coenzyme A, which is how both fat and carbohydrate enter the reactions that burn them. It is spread widely enough across foods that shortfalls are rare.

nutrients.label: Vitamin B6
nutrients.why: The coenzyme for most of what the body does with amino acids, including building the neurotransmitters. It works with folate and B12 to keep homocysteine in check.

nutrients.label: Folate (B9)
nutrients.why: Builds and repairs DNA, so demand rises wherever cells divide fast, which is why it matters most in early pregnancy. Pulses and dark leaves are the richest sources.

nutrients.label: Vitamin B12
nutrients.why: Needed for nerve insulation and for red blood cells, and the one nutrient a plant-based diet cannot supply reliably. No unfortified plant food is a dependable source, so a supplement is standard advice.

nutrients.label: Choline
nutrients.why: Goes into cell membranes and into acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter behind memory and muscle control. The body makes some but rarely enough, and plant sources are thinner than animal ones.

nutrients.label: Betaine
nutrients.why: Spares choline in methylation pathways and concentrated in whole grains, spinach and sugar beet.

nutrients.label: Calcium
nutrients.why: Nearly all of it is in bone, but the small fraction outside runs nerve signalling and muscle contraction, and the body will strip bone to keep that supply steady. Absorption from greens is good except where oxalate binds it.

nutrients.label: Iron
nutrients.why: Carries oxygen in the blood. Plant iron is the non-haem form, absorbed several times less readily than the haem kind, which is why vitamin C in the same meal and tea between meals both change the outcome.

nutrients.label: Magnesium
nutrients.why: A cofactor in several hundred enzymes, including everything that uses ATP, so muscle, nerve and heart rhythm all lean on it. It sits at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule, which is why green leaves carry it.

nutrients.label: Phosphorus
nutrients.why: Most of it is in bone alongside calcium, and the rest is the backbone of DNA and the phosphate groups in ATP. In seeds and grains much of it is locked up as phytate and poorly absorbed.

nutrients.label: Potassium
nutrients.why: The mineral inside cells, balanced against the sodium outside them, and that gradient is what nerve and muscle run on. Whole plant foods are naturally rich in it, the opposite of most processed food.

nutrients.label: Sodium
nutrients.why: Controls fluid balance and, through it, blood pressure. Whole plant foods contain very little, so nearly all of what people eat is added during cooking or processing.

nutrients.label: Zinc
nutrients.why: A cofactor in hundreds of enzymes, and central to immune function and wound healing. Phytate in wholegrains and pulses binds it, so soaking, sprouting and fermenting all raise how much gets through.

nutrients.label: Copper
nutrients.why: Needed to move iron around the body and to build connective tissue, and part of the enzyme that mops up superoxide. Nuts, seeds and cocoa are the richest sources by a distance.

nutrients.label: Manganese
nutrients.why: A cofactor in bone formation, in carbohydrate metabolism, and in the enzyme that protects mitochondria from oxidation. Wholegrains, nuts and tea supply it easily.

nutrients.label: Selenium
nutrients.why: Part of the enzymes that recycle the body's antioxidants and that activate thyroid hormone. Content tracks the soil the plant grew in rather than the plant itself, so figures vary by more than tenfold.

nutrients.label: Beta-carotene
nutrients.why: The orange pigment in carrots and squash, and the main plant source of vitamin A. The body splits it into retinol only as needed, which makes it self-limiting in a way preformed vitamin A is not.

nutrients.label: Alpha-carotene
nutrients.why: A second provitamin A carotenoid, usually found alongside beta-carotene and converted at about half the rate. Carrots, pumpkin and winter squash are where it concentrates.

nutrients.label: Beta-cryptoxanthin
nutrients.why: The third provitamin A carotenoid, and the colour in tangerines, persimmons and red peppers. Converted less efficiently than beta-carotene, though absorbed more readily than it.

nutrients.label: Lutein + zeaxanthin
nutrients.why: The two pigments the retina concentrates into the macula, where they filter blue light. Dark leafy greens and sweetcorn are by far the richest sources. Reported together because assays do not separate them.

nutrients.label: Lycopene
nutrients.why: The red pigment in tomatoes, watermelon and pink guava. Unlike the carotenes it yields no vitamin A, and cooking with a little fat frees far more of it than eating the fruit raw.

nutrients.label: Anthocyanidins
nutrients.why: The red, purple and blue pigments in berries, and the reason a blackberry is not a raspberry. They are what most people mean by antioxidants in fruit, though only a small fraction of what a portion contains is absorbed.

nutrients.label: Flavan-3-ols
nutrients.why: The catechins, which give tea, cocoa and apple skin their astringency. Dark berries and nuts lead this column here, because USDA never measured the full set for cocoa powder and it is withheld rather than undercounted.

nutrients.label: Flavonols
nutrients.why: Quercetin and its relatives, the most widespread flavonoids in vegetables and the best measured of the group. Kale, watercress and onions carry the most of anything here, by a wide margin over the fruit.

nutrients.label: Flavanones
nutrients.why: A class of flavonoids found primarily in citrus fruits (like hesperetin and naringenin) and tomatoes.

nutrients.label: Flavones
nutrients.why: A flavonoid subclass found in high amounts in celery, parsley, and chamomile. They are widely studied for their anti-inflammatory properties.

nutrients.label: Isoflavones
nutrients.why: The phytoestrogens found predominantly in soybeans and soy products. These compounds are structurally similar to estrogen and are actively researched for hormonal health.

nutrients.label: Phytosterols
nutrients.why: Plant cholesterol analogues that block some dietary cholesterol from being absorbed. Seeds and nuts carry by far the most, and USDA has assayed too few foods for this column to be read as a ranking.

nutrients.label: Soluble fibre
nutrients.why: The fibre fraction that dissolves and forms a gel, slowing glucose absorption and feeding gut bacteria. Pectin and beta-glucan both sit inside this figure rather than beside it.

nutrients.label: Insoluble fibre
nutrients.why: The fibre fraction that passes through largely intact, adding bulk and speeding transit. It is usually the larger half of the total fibre figure in whole plant foods.

nutrients.label: Biotin (B7)
nutrients.why: A B vitamin used in fat and glucose metabolism, made partly by gut bacteria. Sources disagree about it more than about any other figure here, so several foods show a range rather than a number.

nutrients.label: Molybdenum
nutrients.why: A trace element that a handful of enzymes use to break down sulphites and purines. The requirement is tiny, deficiency is effectively unknown outside rare genetic disorders, and legumes and grains carry it in quantity.

nutrients.label: Iodine
nutrients.why: Needed to make thyroid hormones, and the widest-spanning figure on this page: seaweed carries thousands of times what any other plant food does, while most were assayed and found to contain none at all. These are Japanese figures, and iodine tracks the soil and the irrigation water as much as the food, so they do not transfer between countries.

nutrients.label: Chromium
nutrients.why: A trace element once believed essential to the way insulin works. The evidence weakened rather than strengthened, and European authorities no longer set an intake for it. These are Japanese figures; older Western ones run ten to fifty times higher, which is contamination from stainless steel during sampling rather than a richer soil.

nutrients.label: Resistant starch
nutrients.why: Starch that survives the small intestine and ferments in the colon, behaving like fibre rather than like carbohydrate. Cooking a starchy food and then cooling it raises the figure, which no composition table can capture.

nutrients.label: Starch
nutrients.why: The bulk of the carbohydrate in grains, legumes and tubers, as distinct from the sugars beside it. These are Japanese figures and the Carbohydrate column is American, so the parts here will not add up to that total.

nutrients.label: Glucose
nutrients.why: Free glucose, already in the form the blood carries, as distinct from the far larger amount locked up in starch and sucrose.

nutrients.label: Fructose
nutrients.why: The sweetest of the common sugars and the one fruit holds most of. It is absorbed more slowly than glucose and handled almost entirely by the liver.

nutrients.label: Sucrose
nutrients.why: Table sugar: one glucose and one fructose bonded together. In these foods it is what the plant stored rather than anything added, and root vegetables and fruit carry the most.

nutrients.label: Maltose
nutrients.why: Two glucose units bonded together, formed when starch is broken down by sprouting, malting or cooking. Most whole plant foods were assayed and found to contain none, which is what this column mostly shows.

nutrients.label: Sorbitol
nutrients.why: A sugar alcohol found in stone fruit and some berries. It is absorbed slowly and incompletely, which is why a large amount of it loosens the bowels.

nutrients.label: Mannitol
nutrients.why: A sugar alcohol, poorly absorbed, so it yields less energy than its weight suggests. Only a few foods here carry a measured figure for it.

nutrients.label: Organic acids, total
nutrients.why: The acids that make fruit and fermented foods taste sharp, added together. They carry a little energy and a great deal of flavour, and the columns beside this one are the largest of them.

nutrients.label: Citric acid
nutrients.why: The dominant acid of citrus fruit and a minor one almost everywhere else. It is what makes a lemon sharp rather than what makes it nourishing.

nutrients.label: Malic acid
nutrients.why: The acid of apples and stone fruit, and named for them. It tastes sharper than citric acid at the same concentration.

nutrients.label: Quinic acid
nutrients.why: An acid of cranberries, coffee and some stone fruit, and the building block a plant starts from when it makes its polyphenols.

nutrients.label: Oxalate, total
nutrients.why: The compound that binds calcium into a form the gut cannot take up, which is why spinach delivers far less calcium than its figure suggests. This is a total, and only the soluble part binds; separating the two needs a source this page does not yet carry.

nutrients.label: Phytate
nutrients.why: Phytate in wholegrains, pulses, nuts and seeds binds iron and zinc in the gut. Soaking, sprouting and fermenting break it down and raise how much gets through.

nutrients.label: Oxalate, soluble
nutrients.why: Soluble oxalate binds to calcium in the gut, making it unavailable. It is the reason the calcium in spinach and chard is poorly absorbed.

nutrients.label: Oxalate, insoluble
nutrients.why: Insoluble oxalate is already bound to calcium before you eat it, and passes straight through. It is excreted without contributing to kidney stones.

nutrients.label: Coenzyme Q10
nutrients.why: A crucial antioxidant and electron carrier in mitochondria, typically synthesized endogenously but heavily supported by dietary intake, especially as endogenous production declines.

nutrients.label: Coenzyme Q9
nutrients.why: The primary isoform of Coenzyme Q in certain plants and rodents. While distinct from CoQ10, it shares antioxidant properties and contributes to total body quinone pools.

nutrients.label: Melatonin
nutrients.why: A hormone universally present in plant matrices (phytomelatonin). It scavenges free radicals and supports the endogenous glutathione system, acting as a potent anti-inflammatory.

nutrients.label: Squalene
nutrients.why: A triterpene and biochemical precursor to the steroid family (including vitamin D and cholesterol), highly concentrated in certain plant oils like olive and argan oil.

nutrients.label: Total Phenolics
nutrients.why: A diverse group of phytochemicals known for their strong antioxidant properties. They help neutralize free radicals and reduce inflammation.

nutrients.name: Beta-glucan
nutrients.why: Soluble fermentable fiber (β-1,3/1,4). Lowers LDL cholesterol, blunts postprandial glucose, and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.
nutrients.label: Beta-glucan

nutrients.name: Pectin
nutrients.why: Structural galacturonic acid polysaccharide. Forms a gel matrix, delaying gastric emptying and fermenting into short-chain fatty acids.
nutrients.label: Pectin

nutrients.name: Inulin / Fructans
nutrients.why: Prebiotic β-(2,1) fructan polymers. Selectively stimulates Bifidobacterium and improves calcium absorption.
nutrients.label: Inulin

nutrients.name: Raffinose
nutrients.why: Non-digestible α-galactooligosaccharide prebiotic.
nutrients.label: Raffinose

nutrients.name: Stachyose
nutrients.why: Non-digestible α-galactooligosaccharide prebiotic.
nutrients.label: Stachyose

nutrients.name: Verbascose
nutrients.why: Non-digestible α-galactooligosaccharide prebiotic.
nutrients.label: Verbascose

nutrients.name: Oligosaccharides
nutrients.why: Total measured non-digestible oligosaccharides (GOS/FOS/RFOs).
nutrients.label: Oligosaccharides

nutrients.name: Lignans
nutrients.why: Phytoestrogenic polyphenols converted by gut microbiota into enterolactone; associated with reduced cardiovascular disease risk.
nutrients.label: Lignans

nutrients.name: Proanthocyanidins
nutrients.why: Condensed tannins (polymeric flavan-3-ols). A-type linkages protect urinary tract mucosa; B-type improve arterial compliance.
nutrients.label: Proanthocyanidins

nutrients.name: Glucosinolates
nutrients.why: Sulfur-rich glycosides. Hydrolyzed by myrosinase into bioactive isothiocyanates (like sulforaphane).
nutrients.label: Glucosinolates

nutrients.name: Glucoraphanin
nutrients.why: The primary precursor to sulforaphane, measured prior to mastication and enzymatic conversion.
nutrients.label: Glucoraphanin

nutrients.name: Ergothioneine
nutrients.why: Unique fungal antioxidant and cytoprotectant actively accumulated in human tissues via a dedicated transporter.
nutrients.label: Ergothioneine

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-4)
nutrients.why: Short-chain Vitamin K2 isomer found primarily in animal products but present in traces in some fermented foods.
nutrients.label: Vitamin K2 (MK-4)

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-7)
nutrients.why: Long-chain Vitamin K2 isomer produced by bacterial fermentation (e.g. Bacillus subtilis in natto).
nutrients.label: Vitamin K2 (MK-7)

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-8)
nutrients.why: Long-chain Vitamin K2 isomer found in fermented vegetables and dairy.
nutrients.label: Vitamin K2 (MK-8)

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-9)
nutrients.why: Long-chain Vitamin K2 isomer found in fermented vegetables.
nutrients.label: Vitamin K2 (MK-9)

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-10)
nutrients.why: Long-chain Vitamin K2 isomer produced by specific bacterial fermentation in dairy and vegetables.
nutrients.label: Vitamin K2 (MK-10)

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2 (Total)
nutrients.why: Total measured menaquinones across all reported isomeric forms.
nutrients.label: Total K2

nutrients.name: Free Inositol
nutrients.why: Key secondary messenger in insulin signal transduction and neurotransmitter regulation.
nutrients.label: Free inositol

nutrients.name: Boron
nutrients.why: Essential ultratrace mineral. Regulates steroid hormone metabolism and enhances bone mineral density. Varies heavily by soil.
nutrients.label: Boron

notes.text: Data for Coenzyme Q10 is compiled from primary research literature (e.g., Venegas 2011, Žmitek 2014, Kubo 2008).
Data for Coenzyme Q9 is compiled from primary research literature.
Data for Melatonin (phytomelatonin) is compiled from primary research literature.
Data for Squalene is compiled from primary research literature.
Data for total oxalate is sourced from the Japanese MEXT 2020 Tables.
Data for insoluble oxalate is sourced from the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT) 2017.
Data for soluble oxalate is sourced from the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT) 2017.
Data for phytate is sourced from the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT) 2017.

Oxalate in this food binds its calcium into a salt the gut cannot take up, so the figure beside this mark is what is present rather than what reaches you. Spinach calcium was absorbed at 5.1 percent against 27.6 percent from milk in the trial that measured it, with its oxalate in slight excess of its calcium, meaning effectively all of it was bound. This is a named exception rather than a survey: a green without this mark has not necessarily been tested.

A low-oxalate brassica, so unusually little of this calcium is bound and an unusually large share of it reaches you. Kale calcium was absorbed at 40.9 percent in the trial that measured it, against 32.1 percent from the milk it was compared with. It is here as the counterpart to the oxalate mark: leafy green is not one category where calcium is concerned, and the two ends of it differ by roughly eightfold.

Added during manufacture, not present in the food itself. Yeast carries no vitamin B12 at all and only modest amounts of the other B vitamins, so the figures here are whatever the maker put in. Plant milks are the same: fortified to whatever level the maker chooses, which is why the packet is the only thing that tells you what is in yours.

USDA published no separate isomer figure for this food, so this value comes from its undifferentiated 18:2 or 18:3 total. In plant foods those are overwhelmingly LA and ALA respectively, so it is a close approximation and the convention the omega-9 column already follows, but it is not a direct measurement of the named fatty acid.
